title: Conjecture 1.2
statement_text: Let $\mathcal{C}$ be a class of connected graphs, closed under contracting edges and subdividing edges. For all $L,C$ there exists $C^{\prime}$ such that if there is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry from a graph $G$ to a member of $\mathcal{C}$, then there is a $(1,C^{\prime})$-quasi-isometry from $G$ to a member of $\mathcal{C}$.
context_text: Graphs may be infinite and have no loops or parallel edges. For graphs $G,H$ and $L,C\ge0$, a map $\phi:V(G)\to V(H)$ is an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry if $\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)+C$ and $\mathrm{dist}_G(u,v)\le L\,\mathrm{dist}_H(\phi(u),\phi(v))+C$ for all $u,v$ (whenever the right-hand distance is finite), and every vertex of $H$ is at distance at most $C$ from $\phi(V(G))$. The conjecture is motivated by the theorem of Chepoi, Dragan, Newman, Rabinovich and Vaxès (also proved by Kerr) that an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry to a tree implies a $(1,C')$-quasi-isometry to a tree, and by a question of Georgakopoulos about planar graphs. Some closure of $\mathcal{C}$ is necessary: subdividing every edge of $H$ once gives a $(2,0)$-quasi-isometry to $H$, and contracting a matching gives a $(3,0)$-quasi-isometry, so $\mathcal{C}$ must be more or less closed under subdivision and contraction. The authors prove that for all $L,C,k$ there is $C'$ such that an $(L,C)$-quasi-isometry from $G$ to a graph $H$ of path-width at most $k$ yields a $(1,C')$-quasi-isometry from $G$ to a graph obtained from $H$ by subdividing and contracting edges (even the same map works after putting integer weights on the edges of $H$), and they can prove the conjecture when $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of connected outerplanar graphs. A result of Davies, Hatzel and Hickingbotham shows that the path-width restriction cannot simply be dropped in the weighted statement, although this does not disprove the conjecture. The case of tree-width at most two is open, even in the weaker form where the target may have tree-width at most some $k$.
paper_title: Asymptotic structure. II. Path-width and additive quasi-isometry
